title: How do you structure a case where the client needs to cut costs?
description: "How can the client cut costs?" The client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage.
hook: Structure a cost case around one equation: cost = how much the client does × resources used per unit × price paid per resource, so every saving comes from needing less, using less or paying less. Ask first which costs are in scope and what must not suffer, then map the cost base and start with the biggest lines. Finish by checking the net saving against the target, not the gross one.
body:
When you will use it

Use it when the client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage ("save 10% in two years"), or when a profitability case turns out to be a cost problem. It is a diagnose question: break the cost base into parts that add up, find the biggest or fastest-growing parts, then work on those. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

Which costs are in scope, how much do we need to save by when, and what must not suffer: quality, safety or service?

The constraint matters as much as the target. A saving that damages service can cost more in lost revenue than it saves.

The structure

  • Need less
    • Stop the activity: close a branch, move a service online
    • Do less of it: lower a service level, such as free next-day delivery
  • Use less per unit
    • Cut waste, errors and rework
    • Get more output per person or machine
  • Pay less per unit
    • Negotiate better prices or consolidate suppliers
    • Switch to cheaper inputs or outsource, such as rail instead of air freight

Make it your own

The three branches map onto the equation: cost = how much we do × resources per unit × price per resource. Each branch cuts one factor, and the factors multiply. That has a practical consequence: savings on two factors do not simply add up. If a factory cuts energy use by 15% and negotiates a 10% lower price on a $20M energy bill, the saving is $20M × (1 − 0.85 × 0.90) = $4.7M, not $5M.

Before applying the tree, ask for the cost base by category and start with the biggest lines. The cost levers tip lists where savings usually hide across a business, from procurement to support functions.

A short worked example

A customer-service team costs $8M a year and management wants a 10% saving, or $800k. The figures are illustrative.

Size the first lever honestly

An automation vendor promises to cut contact-handling time by 20%. But only 60% of the team's costs vary with workload; the rest is managers, systems and premises. The gross saving is $8M × 60% × 20% = $960k. Software licences and oversight cost $300k a year, so the net recurring saving is $660k. That misses the $800k target before counting one-off implementation and training costs.

Add an independent lever, and check the overlap

Many contacts are avoidable, such as customers calling about confusing bills. Suppose clearer billing removes 10% of contacts: that saves $8M × 60% × 10% = $480k, for $100k a year of system cost.

Now the overlap. Automation applies to the contacts that remain, so its saving falls to $8M × 60% × 90% × 20% ≈ $864k. Combined gross saving: $480k + $864k = $1,344k, not the $1,440k you get by adding the two levers separately. Net of $400k of running costs, the programme saves about $944k, clearing the target with some room. Fixing the cause of calls also improves the customer experience, which automation alone does not.

Protect what matters

Track first-contact resolution and complaint escalations as each lever rolls out. If customers call back because the bot did not solve their problem, the saving disappears.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer announces cuts:

They should automate with AI, move staff offshore and reduce headcount.

A strong answer sizes them net, against the target:

Automation saves about $960k gross, but after $300k of software costs it's $660k, which is short of the $800k target. I'd pair it with fixing the billing issues that cause avoidable calls.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Brainstorming before mapping the cost base. Find where the money goes first.
  2. Reporting gross savings. Subtract the new running costs, and list one-off costs separately.
  3. Adding overlapping levers. When levers act on the same volume, apply one after the other.
  4. Cutting costs that bring in revenue. Sales staff and service quality often pay for themselves.

Practise with real prompts

1. A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show the answer
  • Number of returns: did online orders grow? Return rate by category, size and brand; serial returners.
  • Cost per return: shipping, handling, refurbishing, items that can no longer be sold.
  • Why customers return: fit and sizing, photos and descriptions, ordering several sizes on purpose.
  • Policy: free returns, the return window, exchanges first.

Where to start: orders × return rate × cost per return. Find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: listing policy changes before splitting the number of returns from the cost per return.

2. A retail bank wants to cut operating costs by 15% in two years.

Show the answer
  • Branches: number, size and use; staffing against footfall.
  • Operations: payments, lending and account opening in the back office; automation and outsourcing.
  • Technology: old systems, licences, data centres, duplicate vendors.
  • Support functions: HR, finance, procurement; layers of management.

Where to start: the biggest cost pool first, usually staff in branches and operations.

The trap: listing ideas without sizing the cost base, so you cannot say which matters.

3. A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show the answer
  • Unit economics per order: commission, delivery fee, courier cost, discounts and refunds.
  • Marketing: cost to acquire a customer against their value; promotions with no repeat orders.
  • Cities: profit by city; pause the weakest.
  • Fixed costs: head office, tech, hiring plans.

Where to start: profit per order by city. If every order loses money, volume makes it worse.

The trap: cutting head office first when the loss is in every order.
